claims.text: Intrinsic lattice distortions from high configurational disorder contribute to the anomalous stress–strain response of HfNbTaTiZr.
Local thermal-expansion heterogeneities generate internal residual stresses that govern the alloy's anomalous thermoelastic response.
Controlled high-temperature annealing will homogenize the microstructure, relieve residual stresses, and reduce local expansion mismatches.
Reducing residual stresses and expansion mismatches will produce a more conventional temperature-dependent response.
The initial as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single phase.
The initial alloy contains compositional heterogeneities.
The initial alloy contains lattice-parameter heterogeneities.
Compositional and lattice-parameter differences cause local variations in thermal expansion.
Local thermal-expansion variations create internal residual-stress fields.
Residual stresses impede dislocation motion in the as-cast alloy.
Residual stresses stabilize the alloy's elastic moduli against temperature-dependent changes.
The refractory HEA exhibits high room-temperature yield strength, elevated-temperature softening resistance, and unusually weak temperature dependence of elastic anisotropic deformation.
Annealing will allow intrinsic lattice-distortion effects to dominate after residual stresses are reduced.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, annealed HfNbTaTiZr will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, annealed HfNbTaTiZr will have higher elevated-temperature creep rates.
Annealed HfNbTaTiZr will show less hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
Annealed HfNbTaTiZr will show a more conventional temperature dependence of elastic modulus between 293 and approximately 1100 K.
The effects of residual-stress relief should be most evident from approximately 600–1250 °C in aging and creep tests and from 293–1100 K in elastic-modulus tests.
Earlier cited work establishes baseline behavior across tensile creep, cold rolling, elastic-modulus measurements, and aging treatments.
